brut.title: Claims Five: The Quinlans and their surprisingly well-backed ...

webpage.text:
Claims Five: The Quinlans and their surprisingly well-backed winners | Horse racing

A winner at Wolverhampton on Tuesday caught my eye (after the race, alas). He was trained by Noel Quinlan, brother of Michael. The two men are based in Newmarket and have had some high-profile successes, winning the Queen Mary at Royal Ascot and the Fred Winter at the Cheltenham Festival, but mostly it seems that they are incredibly dangerous with well-backed runners in low-quality handicaps.

Michael used to hold the licence in his name but it was passed to Noel earlier this year. As far as I know, the operation works in much the same way as it has ever done.

Ensnare, their winner on Tuesday, was the latest to follow a pattern that makes the Quinlans hard to love, from a punter's perspective. I have collected five examples below.

Broadly, their common features are these. The horse has shown some ability in the past but now seems to have lost it, running very badly for several months. During that time, he drops a long way through the weights, yet starts at ever bigger odds.

Then, a day comes when it seems that everyone wants to back him and he starts favourite or close to it. The money is right; he runs much better than his recent form and wins or is narrowly beaten.

Afterwards, there is always something to which connections can point that explains the improved showing. The horse will have had a recent break and be better for it, or will have had treatment for some ailment. The distance of the race will be shorter or longer than for his latest disappointment, or he may be wearing some kind of headgear for the first time.

Whatever the detail, it is enough to dissuade the incurious stewards from holding a formal inquiry. The Quinlans accept the congratulations of those present, who can be sure that something similar will happen again before long.

Horse racing in this country depends for a large part of its income on the willingness of punters to bet on all levels of the sport, but it seems to me that you could hardly blame a gambler for leaving low-quality races alone if this is the kind of thing that can happen without the authorities taking an interest. When a horse wins in these circumstances, you have basically no chance of picking it unless you decide to follow the money.

In my republic, connections would be required to state on the morning of a race any factor which they thought might result in an improved effort from their runner, with the information being published on a website and in betting shops. If no such factor was stated but the horse was well-backed and won, there would be hideous consequences for those concerned.

But we do not live in my republic and are the poorer for it. Neither the stewards nor the British Horseracing Authority will protect us, it seems, so we must do what we can to protect ourselves. Take note of these examples and be wary for anything similar in future.

The Quinlans, of course, have not made the world in which they work. It is hard to make ends meet in this game, yet it appears that they have a collection of satisfied owners and that makes them much better trainers than all those others who hardly win a race from one month to the next.

But they can hardly expect punters to admire them for winning in this way. If their owners have made a few quid, it will have come from people like us who imagined the form book could be trusted.

Again, they are hardly the only trainers who sometimes win races in these circumstances, but they have done it enough times to catch my eye. Perhaps I'm wrong, though, and each one of these horses was backable on the basis only of the pre-race information. If you happened to profit from any of them, do let me know through the comments below.

I should say that, in three of these cases, I have no direct knowledge as to whether the Quinlans or their owners placed any bets. Noel Quinlan has said that he backed both Bishopbriggs and Tell Halaf.


1) Royal Island, December 2008


Royal Island had started out with Mark Johnston, for whom he was second in the 2004 Woodcote Stakes and again in the 2006 Lincoln, off a mark of 99. He was sold to Michael Cunningham's yard in Ireland but spring 2008 found him back in England, trained by Michael Quinlan.

On his first start for his new connections, he was fourth of nine at Newmarket in mid-May, prompting the Racing Post's analyst to note that he was "handicapped to win at his best". He was on a rating of 84 that day.

Four further defeats saw him dropped another half-stone. Then, he hacked up in a seller at Chepstow but the handicapper was so unimpressed that he was another 2lb lower for his next start.

From 28 August to 2 November, Royal Island ran another eight times but seemed to be losing his form, starting at increasingly long odds and getting beaten further from one run to the next.

When he showed up at Wolverhampton on 6 December, there was little enough reason to fancy him, except that he was now running off 57, two stones below the rating for his Newmarket run seven months before. Then again he'd been stuffed four times over the same course and distance over the previous two months.

This time was different. "Well backed" according to the Post, he went off as the 2-1 favourite, took it up with a furlong to run and was soon clear before being eased down to win by two lengths.

If you want a reason why he may have improved on recent performances, you could look at the fact that he had had a month's break before this run, the first time he'd had such a gap since his Chepstow seller. Then again, he had a month off before his next run and finished last of 13.

It was the start of another bad run. He was never better than ninth in any of his next seven starts and was 33-1 or bigger for the last four of them.

Then, in September 2009, history came close to repeating itself. Despite his woeful form over the previous nine months, Royal Island went back to Wolverhampton, was the subject of "strong market support throughout the day" (the Post), started as 2-1 favourite and ran really well, being beaten by just half a length.

Punters everywhere were doubtless gutted that the gamble had not quite come off this time.


2) Tallest Peak, December 2009


The four-year-old Tallest Peak had raced 10 times without success when he ran at Wolverhampton, eight days before Christmas. For his three starts the previous month, he had been 16-1, 9-1 and 28-1 and had finished ninth (in a seller), ninth and 13th (of 13).

Why might he do better this time? Well, he was down to a mark of 49, 9lb below his original rating from his first handicap run seven months before. He was wearing blinkers for the first time and stepping back to seven furlongs, the distance at which he had been a decent third at Kempton in September.

"Well supported" according to the Post, he started at 7-2 and won by four lengths, looking well ahead of the handicapper. Still, that effort now seems a one-off, since he was beaten in four starts over the next month and has not raced since.


3) Bishopbriggs, December 2010


Bishopbriggs had won a couple of races at Wolverhampton in January 2010, not long after joining the yard from John Ryan. The second of those wins came off a mark of 58 and he was raised to 63 but, after a losing run of eight races, had dropped back down to 54 by the following winter.

And he really lost those eight races. On his next start after winning, he was eighth of eight, then ninth of nine, tenth of 11 and tenth of 12. In his four runs after that, he was never better than seventh and started at 25-1 or bigger each time.

At Lingfield on the day before New Year's Eve, he was still 12-1 half an hour before the race but was then heavily backed and started as the 11-4 favourite. Making most of the running, he pulled clear in the final quarter-mile to win by four lengths.

The stipendiary steward noted an explanation from Noel Quinlan that the horse's back problem had been treated since his previous start three months before. Quinlan also said that the yard had been out of form for much of the year. This was enough to dissuade the stewards from holding a formal inquiry into the improved form.


4) Tell Halaf, December 2010


Just half an hour after Bishopbriggs, the Quinlans pulled off the same feat with Tell Halaf, for whom market support emerged at the same time as for his stablemate. Having been a 7-1 shot, he started as the 9-4 favourite and won almost as comfortably as Bishopbriggs, albeit cheekily by just half a length.

Tell Halaf had raced respectably through the first half of the year when trained by Michael Bell, winning at Lingfield in May off 63. But he seemed to lose the plot after joining the Quinlans in July, finishing 10th, 11th, 10th, 10th, 10th and ninth on his first six starts for them.

Then came the Lingfield race and sudden success. By this time, he was running off 54, 20lb below the last mark he'd had when racing for Bell.

In six previous runs for the Quinlans, Tell Halaf had not got within 13 lengths of a winner. Still, the stewards were not moved to hold an inquiry, being reassured by the trainer's statement that the yard was in better form than when he had last raced, two months before.

"I didn't go into the stewards' at all," Noel Quinlan told me the next day. "The stipe took notes off me, took them to the stewards and they've accepted my explanations. I couldn't see why they wouldn't. We're talking about shit, low-grade handicaps."

He admitted to having had "four £20 each-way doubles" on Tell Halaf and Bishopbriggs at odds of 8-1 and 7-1, which would generate a total profit of around £6,000. "Four or five owners have made a few quid," he added.

"Are we not supposed to back horses now? We do whatever owners want us to do. If they send us a horse and say, tell me when he's really, really ready and get him in the worst race possible, that's what we'll try and do."


5) Ensnare, July 2011


And so to Tuesday's race, by which time the licence had been switched from Michael to Noel. Ensnare, the beast in question, had won three races for Ian Williams before passing through Jeff Pearce's yard to join the Quinlans early this year.

This week's race was Ensnare's fifth for the stable. In his first four, he started at 20-1 or bigger and finished twelfth of 13, twelfth of 13, tenth of 10 and eighth of nine. He raced out the back through all four races and never got within 11 lengths of the winner.

At Wolverhampton on Tuesday, having dropped a stone in the weights since joining the Quinlans, he raced prominently, hit the front two furlongs out and pulled two and three-quarter lengths clear of the opposition. He was returned at 11-2 after "proving strong in the market throughout the day" (the Post).

The Quinlans do not appear to have been present. Their representative told reporters that the horse "has had a break and has freshened up at home. He was ridden more prominently this time and the drop back in trip has helped as well".

As to that drop back in trip, Tuesday's race was over seven furlongs, which is indeed shorter than the mile of his previous run. On the other hand, he had been stuffed on his two runs before that, both over seven furlongs.

The same representative told the stewards that Ensnare had benefited from a two-month break since his previous run and from the use of a blindfold in the stalls, credited with helping him get a better position from the outset.

Presented with this information, the stewards opted not to hold an inquiry. Frankly, that seems a mistake to me and counts as yet another step towards a future in which no one trusts the lower tier of our sport enough to risk their money on it.

webpage.text:
Prince Bishop reigns at Dubai World Cup

Julian Muscat

Sat, 28 March 2015 at 6:36 pm UTC

Prince Bishop left racing fans scratching their heads when he cut down the rags-to-riches American horse California Chrome to win the $10 million Dubai World Cup on Saturday.It was a stunning outcome at the world's richest race, and one virtually unforseen by the 60,000 spectators at Meydan racecourse.The stage looked set for California Chrome to join a hallowed cast of previous winners when jockey Victor Espinosa moved his mount into a challenging position rounding the turn for home.But jockey William Buick aboard Prince Bishop had other ideas.Having countered Espinosa's move, Buick drove his mount past the sentimental favourite en route to a decisive victory by 2 3/4 lengths.The second American challenger, Lea, finished third, one place ahead of local hope Candy Boy."I don't go numb very often but I can't explain what I'm feeling right now," Buick said. "This is just nuts."It was the fourth time Prince Bishop, who is trained in Dubai by Saeed Bin Suroor, had contested the World Cup.He finished ninth last year, seventh in 2012 and tenth the previous year.His victory earned his owner, Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohd al Maktoum of the Dubai ruling family, the winner's purse of $6 million.Bin Suroor was posting his seventh triumph in the race. He won it 12 months ago with African Story but that horse could finish only sixth this time under Bin Suroor's senior jockey, James Doyle.Japan's pair of champions, Hokko Tarumae and Epiphaneia, could finish only fifth and last respectively in the nine-runner field.- 'ran his eyeballs out' -Art Sherman, who trains California Chrome, was magnanimous in defeat."Second money is not bad at all," he said."He ran his eyeballs out. He was right there in contention all the way."The horse you think is going to win doesn't always. That's what happens in this game."Espinosa was equally philosophical."He (California Chrome) kind of lost his stride a little bit on the home turn because the horse on my inside (Hokko Tarumae) pushed me out. But overall, he ran awesome."Prince Bishop's victory was unexpected because he had run on Maydan's dirt surface twice before and resented the sand kickback that sprays horses in the face. However, he had finished strongly once he found clear air.Buick's role in his World Cup victory was pivotal. He had ridden Prince Bishop on his last two starts and recognised the importance of having a clear track ahead of him."Saeed told me to avoid getting kickback if at all possible," the jockey related."I knew that that was the best way to maximise my horse's chance. He has a very unorthodox way of racing but he ran on well to the end."Buick forged his path to victory when he secured a place on the outside of the field from his inside gate draw in stall one.He was always within striking distance of a gallop dictated by Hokko Tarumae and pounced on California Chrome early in the home straight.An eight-year-old horse, Prince Bishop is the oldest winner of the Dubai World Cup.This was his eleventh victory from 28 starts. It was by some way the most significant.

brut.title: Skippylongstocking Repeats in Charles Town Classic - BloodHorse

webpage.text:
Skippylongstocking Repeats in Charles Town Classic

Trainer Saffie Joseph Jr. also won the Charles Town Oaks (G2) with Mystic Lake.

 * August 24, 2024

Replicating if not somewhat surpassing his victory in the 2023 Charles Town Classic Stakes (G2), Daniel Alonso's Skippylongstocking  took charge in the $1 million, 1 1/8-mile race Aug. 23 and scored a blowout victory over longshots Velocitor  and Komorebino Omoide .

The winner's time of 1:50.34, about a second and a half off the track record, was quicker than his 2023 clocking of 1:51.37, and his margin of victory was somewhat larger than last year. He crossed the wire 5 3/4 lengths in front after winning by five lengths last summer.

Even the manner of his victory was similar. He sped to the front under Jose Ortiz in the three-turn race on the six-furlong oval at Hollywood Casino at Charles Town Races and asserted his superiority. Clear by a length for much of the race over Frosted Departure , who would ultimately weaken to seventh, he turned aside bids from stalking rivals Velocitor and Komorebino Omoide on the final turn before drawing away.

The Saffie Joseph Jr. trainee earned $564,000 for his Friday night victory, boosting his earnings to $2,992,985. He is 9-2-5 in 26 starts. He returned $4.20 to win as the heavy favorite in the field of 10. Joseph's other starter, Lord Miles , finished last in the field of 10.

Skippylongstocking's effort followed a fifth-place finish in the Aug. 3 Whitney Stakes (G1) at Saratoga Race Course, where he weakened after chasing victorious Arthur's Ride🔥   through fast fractions.

Last year, he followed up the Charles Town Classic with a third-place finish behind Cody's Wish🔥   and National Treasure🔥   in the Breeders' Cup Dirt Mile (G1) at Santa Anita Park. Most of his experience has come in races from a mile to 1 1/8 miles.

Classic-placed Skippylongstocking, bred in Kentucky by Brushy Hill, is a 5-year-old son of Exaggerator  out of the War Chant mare Twinkling , a producer of three stakes winners from four foals to race. He was a $37,000 purchase by his owner from the Top Line Sales consignment at the 2021 Ocala Breeders' Spring Sale of 2-Year-Olds in Training.

The 2016 Preakness Stakes (G1) winner, Exaggerator stood this past season for $5,000 at Elite Thoroughbreds in Louisiana.


Video: Charles Town Classic S. (G2)

More Joseph Success

Another Joseph trainee, Mystic Lake , excelled in the race preceding the Charles Town Classic, taking the $750,000 Charles Town Oaks (G2) over seven furlongs. After tracking the early pace, she took over and pulled away by 5 3/4 lengths, timed in 1:24.18 under Hall of Fame jockey Mike Smith. She paid $14 to win.


The 3-year-old daughter of Mo Town , bred in Florida by Peggy Costanzo out of the Itsmyluckyday  mare Salty Soul, races for owners C2 Racing Stable and Stefania Farms. In earning her second graded stakes win this year, she is 5-3-1 in 11 career starts with earnings of $758,554.

Grade 2 winner My Mane Squeeze , outpaced early and hung wide and bumped entering the first turn, rallied to grab second over Princess Madison🔥 .


Video: Charles Town Oaks (G2)
